Their thermal differences measure response after one calibration; they do not demonstrate thermal differences between equally refitted branches.

That study varied fitted parameter combinations, whereas the present continuations retain the source factor of the LL length fit. Their contrast measures material-function response after a common calibration. Together these designs show the distinct roles of geometric fitting and temperature information in assessing a model.

before: The effective-heat-capacity representation separates latent and sensible storage~\cite{vanelsen2007}. Applied to the adopted linear phase law, it explains why the local storage perturbation is much smaller than the sensible-$c_p$ perturbation. Inside the phase interval, the fixed latent term contributes 4666.67~\si{\joule\per\kilogram\per\kelvin} to effective specific heat. At 1320~$^\circ$C, holding sensible $c_p$ reduces it by 7.09\%, but reduces latent-inclusive effective specific heat by only 0.95\% and enthalpy from the cold reference by 0.66\%. The conductivity reduction at the same temperature is 22.48\%. These comparisons show that the two nominal property changes perturb transport and total storage by different amounts. They do not isolate latent heat as the cause: latent heat is unchanged in all corners, and each continuation starts below the solidus, so pre-melting enthalpy and the temperature--enthalpy inverse also change.
after: The effective-heat-capacity representation separates latent and sensible storage~\cite{vanelsen2007}. In the adopted phase interval, latent heat contributes 4666.67~\si{\joule\per\kilogram\per\kelvin} to effective specific heat. The 7.09\% sensible-$c_p$ reduction at 1320~$^\circ$C consequently becomes a 0.95\% change in latent-inclusive effective specific heat and a 0.66\% change in enthalpy from the cold reference, compared with the 22.48\% conductivity reduction at the same temperature. This energy accounting explains the unequal local perturbation sizes applied to transport and storage. All branches retain the same latent heat; changing sensible heat capacity also changes pre-melting enthalpy and the temperature--enthalpy inverse because its continuation begins below the solidus.
purpose: State the actual relation/process and keep consequential scope at its interpretation point.

before: The diagnostics support a changed balance between coordinate enthalpy transport and diffusion, but do not support equating conductivity holding with reduced integrated outward heat flow from the selected rear region. The selected axial-face P\'eclet diagnostic increases under conductivity holding, but the integrated rear-region conductive power also increases (Section~\ref{sec:property-results}). Lower conductivity therefore does not imply lower integrated outward heat flow in this comparison; both the temperature gradients and the boundary of the temperature-selected region change. Surface recovery also changes consistently through $K(T)$ and its inverse. The resolved tail displacement is a response of the complete conduction model and observation operator. Assigning it solely to suppressed bulk heat escape would require a matched-region flux comparison or a separation of field and recovery contributions.
after: Conductivity holding changes the local transport balance and the temperature gradients together. The selected axial-face P\'eclet diagnostic increases, and the integrated rear-region conductive power also increases (Section~\ref{sec:property-results}). The latter is evaluated over a temperature-selected boundary that moves with the solution, providing a counterexample to equating a smaller conductivity with lower integrated outward power from that region. Surface recovery changes consistently through $K(T)$ and its inverse. The resolved tail displacement thus combines the field response and the threshold-recovery operator. A matched-region flux comparison or separation of field and recovery contributions would distinguish their respective roles.
purpose: State the actual relation/process and keep consequential scope at its interpretation point.

after: Rear-boundary location, phase separation and material time describe different aspects of the calibrated field. The B/C rear phase spans are 80.26 and 80.79~\um{}, while passage times are 100.33 and 67.33~\us{} as scan speed rises from 0.8 to 1.2~m/s (Fig.~\ref{fig:trends}). before: Thermography distinguishes these questions experimentally. Hooper~\cite{hooper2018} measured both centerline spatial profiles and temperature histories at fixed build-plate locations, including pulsed scans and turn events. Those observations show why a spatial profile and a thermal history cannot be exchanged without accounting for the scan motion. Lane's cooling-rate exemplars~\cite{lane2020} use a below-solidus interval and a different rear-boundary definition, so they do not validate the present 1350--1290~$^\circ$C interval. A comparison would require a temperature trajectory over the same interval, with scan position, exposure and observation mapping included.
after: Spatial profiles and material temperature histories also have distinct measurement roles. Thermography has resolved centerline profiles together with fixed-location temperature histories through scan pulses and turn events~\cite{hooper2018}. The AMMT analysis converts position to time at a known constant speed, using a below-solidus temperature interval and its radiance-based boundary definition~\cite{lane2020}. Aligning a measured trajectory with the present 1350--1290~$^\circ$C calculation would require the same temperature interval and explicit treatment of scan position, exposure and observation mapping.
purpose: State the actual relation/process and keep consequential scope at its interpretation point.

before: The passage transformation describes stationary material crossing the assumed steady field. Fluid trajectories can sample a different thermal path: in a Ni--20Cr dispersion-strengthened alloy, melt-flow calculations produced narrower near-surface peaks and hotter subsurface excursions than an unmodified conduction field~\cite{Hou2024Dissolution}. That material and flow model do not validate the present IN625 interval, but show why $\ell_m/v$ cannot be equated with liquid residence or a nonequilibrium freezing path. This boundary matters when thermal outputs are used for microstructure: Plotkowski et al.~\cite{Plotkowski2017Rapid} treated melt-pool geometry verification separately from solidification-condition calculations and an experimental grain-structure comparison. Their AlSi10Mg/IN718 study provides a useful methodological distinction, not validation of this IN625 model. Here, neither grain morphology nor segregation has been tested, and the rear passage interval remains a model diagnostic. In transient multi-line calculations, interface velocity can also depart from beam velocity~\cite{Plotkowski2017Rapid}; the present $v$-based conversion is restricted to a straight, quasi-steady track.
after: The passage transformation follows stationary material crossing the assumed steady field. Fluid motion adds another path through the thermal field: calculations for a Ni--20Cr dispersion-strengthened alloy produced narrower near-surface temperature peaks and hotter subsurface excursions than the corresponding unmodified conduction histories~\cite{Hou2024Dissolution}. This distinction links thermal-field assessment to the trajectories used in microstructure models. A separate transient-conduction study connected geometry verification, solidification-condition calculations and an experimental grain-structure comparison for AlSi10Mg laser and IN718 electron-beam cases~\cite{Plotkowski2017Rapid}. It also showed interface velocities governed by hatch progression in overlapping multi-line melts. The present $v$-based conversion applies to a straight, quasi-steady track and characterizes its centerline passage interval; flow-dependent paths and grain/segregation predictions require their corresponding physical descriptions and measurements.
purpose: State the actual relation/process and keep consequential scope at its interpretation point.

before: The shape residual does not identify a unique missing mechanism. An alternative source is a substantive explanation: Coleman et al.~\cite{dynamic2024} calibrated a dynamic volumetric source for bare IN625 at 195~W and 800~mm/s over several spot sizes, then applied it to a layer case. Their source adjusts depth and effective absorption with the local melt-pool state; their phase-dependent properties and 1410~K eutectic endpoint also differ from the present equilibrium interval. A comparison using the same measured beam, phase assumptions, calibration target and geometry operators would distinguish source redistribution from the effect of a different material closure. An imaging replay is a cheaper first test of how the radiance-to-threshold mismatch changes the fitted source factor. Neither comparison is supplied by the present continuation corners.
after: Source distribution and effective transport remain competing explanations for the shape residual. A dynamic volumetric source calibrated on bare IN625 tracks at 195~W and 800~mm/s across several spot sizes was subsequently applied to a layer case~\cite{dynamic2024}. The source adjusts its depth and effective absorption with the local melt-pool state, while its phase-dependent properties and 1410~K eutectic endpoint differ from the present interval. Matching the beam, phase assumptions, calibration target and geometry operators would make source redistribution and material closure directly comparable. Replaying the imaging operator would first quantify the effect of radiance-derived boundaries on the fitted source factor.
purpose: State the actual relation/process and keep consequential scope at its interpretation point.

before: Two physical limits govern the thermal interpretation. First, the supplier property tables end at 982~$^\circ$C for $k$ and 1093~$^\circ$C for $c_p$, below the solidus~\cite{specialmetals625}. The L/H branches are continuation scenarios, not measured liquid-state functions. Composition-based Ni-superalloy estimates explicitly include IN625 conductivity, but the underlying liquid-state data remain limited~\cite{mills2006}. Such estimates provide candidates for a material-specific comparison; they do not select either continuation for this coupon. Second, the model excludes evaporation, melt flow and surface evolution. Its LL, HL, LH and HH surface peaks are approximately 2697, 3507, 2756 and 3721~$^\circ$C. In particular, the held-conductivity peaks cannot be interpreted as credible physical-temperature predictions from this balance. The model nevertheless exposes how those assumptions affect the fitted geometry and rear thresholds.
after: High-temperature material data and omitted liquid-state processes bound the physical use of these sensitivities. The supplier tables end at 982~$^\circ$C for $k$ and 1093~$^\circ$C for $c_p$~\cite{specialmetals625}; L/H extends them by two prescribed rules. Composition-based estimates include IN625 conductivity and identify limited underlying liquid-state data~\cite{mills2006}, providing candidates for a material-specific comparison. The present conduction balance also omits evaporation, melt flow and surface evolution. Its LL, HL, LH and HH positive-$y$ surface-sample peaks are approximately 2697, 3507, 2756 and 3721~$^\circ$C. The extreme held-conductivity temperatures make the absent liquid-state processes consequential; those peaks serve as sensitivity outputs of the assumed balance, while independent thermal measurements are needed to establish their physical credibility.
purpose: State the actual relation/process and keep consequential scope at its interpretation point.

The analytical benchmark, energy balance and solution correction assess numerical execution. Physical comparison additionally depends on the calibration history, separately sampled length and cross-section populations, and source-specific measurement-uncertainty scales described in Section~2.1.
